newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end slightly lower amid heavy volume.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end slightly lower amid heavy volume.

text.p: U.S. government securities prices closed weaker on Thursday, little changed from Wednesday's prices following a day of heavy trading volume.

"We're stuck in a range until we see some numbers of some importance tomorrow," said Wayne Ayers, chief economist at Bank of Boston. "If retail sales come in much above consensus it won't be taken well after the Fed's comments in March."
The Federal Open Market Committee issued a statement when it tightened monetary policy at its March 25 meeting and hinted more such moves were possible.
Ayers said next week's consumer price index was likely to affect markets more markets than Friday's producer price data.
"We're at a stage where we have some asymmetry here. A good number won't give us much of a lift a bad number will cause a large reaction," Ayers said.

The FOMC next meets on May 20 and market expectations were growing that a further 25-basis-point tightening of monetary policy was in the cards, especially should consumer spending continue at high levels. Under Chairman Alan Greenspan, the Fed has never tightened once and then failed to follow up with further moves.

"Retail sales could come in a little bit weaker than people are expecting. The number may understate that the level of consumer spending probably is not as strong in the second quarter as it was in the first," said Richard Berner, executive vice president and chief economist at Mellon Bank Corp. Still, consumer spending will remain strong, he said.
Berner said next week's reading on CPI may come in stronger than expected, led not just by higher air fares but a number of other factors as well.
He also saw strength in the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Employment Cost Index set for release on March 29.

Berner said the ECI was a better indicator of employment conditions than monthly nonfarm payrolls as it covered most U.S. occupations. He saw wage growth at less than the 4.0 percent seen in in the March quarterly ECI -- most likely at 3.5 percent to 3.6 percent. "But that's still high," he added.

"Wages are accelerating and the issue really is are companies able to pass along price increases," Berner said. "Some will try because demand continues to look very strong." He saw further tightening in May and didn't expect that the Fed would pause before a fed funds rate of 6.0 percent was seen.
For the second straight session activity was higher in the 10-year sector than the two-year area and volume was heavy.

"The ($2.5 billion) J.C. Penney deal (priced Wednesday) only went as low as a three-year tranche and that may explain a lot of the activity today. And, although it's an extremely inefficient hedge, there was a 10-year TIPs (inflation-indexed bonds) auction this week," said a trader a primary dealership.
He said talk also was that one or two primary dealerships had acquired large positions of old (October 2006) 10-year paper and then were liquidating the issues.
Trading of when-issued three-year bills also was more than four times higher than usual, according to GovPX.

The Treasury's 30-year bond closed off 3/32 at 94-even to yield 7.11 percent. The 10-year note closed down 2/32 at 95-11/32, yielding 6.91 percent. The five-year note traded off 2/32 at 99-12/32 to yield 6.77 percent. The two-year note closed down 1/32 at 99-21/32, yielding 6.44 percent.
The three-month bill ended up five basis points at 5.14 percent; the six-month bill was up three basis points at 5.38 percent and the year bill was up one basis point at 5.64 percent.
